# Heartwood

> Nostr private keys are pasted into web apps, stored in browser extensions, and copied to the clipboard. Heartwood keeps them on dedicated hardware instead.

Heartwood is open-source Nostr signing built on nsec-tree. `heartwood-bridge` is a headless, keyless daemon that connects Nostr relays to a USB-tethered hardware signer -- an ESP32 running the [heartwood-esp32](https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood-esp32) firmware, or a Ledger running the [heartwood-ledger](https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood-ledger) app. The bridge holds no key material and never sees plaintext: NIP-44 decryption, NIP-46 request dispatch, per-client permissions, session/replay protection, and signing all happen on the device itself, inline over USB. The bridge is only the device's relay connection, and nothing more.

It is aimed at Nostr power users who want hardware-backed key security without renting a VPS, and at app developers building multi-identity Nostr clients that need a signing backend which works on iOS, Android, and web equally, since NIP-46 is relay-mediated.

Heartwood is a direct replacement for nsecBunker (no VPS required), an iOS-compatible alternative to Amber (Android-only), and a multi-identity alternative to LNbits NSD (one key per device). The distinguishing feature is unlinkable-by-default multi-identity: one seed on the hardware signer derives unlimited separate identities that cannot be correlated by an observer unless you deliberately prove the link.

## Getting Started

Two pieces: a hardware signer and a bridge host (any small Linux box with a USB port and a network connection -- a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W or similar). The signer is either an ESP32 running `heartwood-esp32` (default `serial` transport; keys provisioned over USB via [Sapwood](https://sapwood.forgesworn.dev) or the offline `provision` CLI) or a Ledger running `heartwood-ledger` (`HEARTWOOD_TRANSPORT=ledger-tcp` or `ledger-hid`; no `bridge.secret`). Real-device status for Ledger: `ledger-tcp` is proven end to end against the Speculos emulator only; `ledger-hid` (a physical Ledger over Linux hidraw) is implemented and its USB framing is unit-tested, but it has not been verified on physical hardware, so treat real Ledger devices as untested.

Install the bridge:

```bash
curl -sL https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo bash
```

The installer creates the `heartwood` user, `/var/lib/heartwood` and an enabled but not started `heartwood-bridge` unit, with `HEARTWOOD_SERIAL_PORT` pre-filled from the first `/dev/ttyUSB*` or `/dev/ttyACM*` it finds (else `/dev/ttyUSB0`). Re-running it rewrites the unit file, so put your settings in a drop-in:

```bash
sudo systemctl edit heartwood-bridge
# add:
#   [Service]
#   Environment=HEARTWOOD_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0
#   Environment=HEARTWOOD_RELAYS=wss://relay.damus.io,wss://nos.lol
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now heartwood-bridge
```

Docker instead (multi-arch image; pass the device through and mount the data directory; `<version>` is a release version without the leading `v`, or `main`):

```bash
docker run -d --name heartwood-bridge --restart unless-stopped \
  --device /dev/ttyUSB0 \
  -e HEARTWOOD_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  -e HEARTWOOD_RELAYS=wss://relay.damus.io,wss://nos.lol \
  -v /var/lib/heartwood:/var/lib/heartwood \
  ghcr.io/forgesworn/heartwood:<version>
```

### Configuration

Environment variables win over `config.json` (keys `transport`, `serial_port`, `relays`) in the data directory; a missing or malformed `config.json` is ignored. The binary takes no arguments apart from `--version`, `--help` and `--bunker-uri`.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `HEARTWOOD_SERIAL_PORT` | none (required) | Signer address: a serial device path (`/dev/ttyUSB0`) for `serial`, `host:port` for `ledger-tcp`, `/dev/hidrawN` or `auto` for `ledger-hid` |
| `HEARTWOOD_TRANSPORT` | `serial` | `serial` (ESP32), `ledger-tcp` or `ledger-hid` (Ledger) |
| `HEARTWOOD_DATA_DIR` | `/var/lib/heartwood` | Directory holding `config.json` and `bridge.secret` |
| `HEARTWOOD_RELAYS` | built-in `DEFAULT_RELAYS` (see `crates/heartwood-bridge/src/config.rs`) | Comma-separated relay URLs |

### Provisioning

For the `serial` transport, `<HEARTWOOD_DATA_DIR>/bridge.secret` must exist before the bridge will start: 64 hex characters (whitespace ignored) or exactly 32 raw bytes, mode 0600, owned by the user that runs the bridge. Sapwood (browser) or the `provision` CLI (offline; lives in the [heartwood-esp32](https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood-esp32) repo, not this one) produce it on the machine they run on. If that is not the bridge host, copy it across:

```bash
sudo install -m 0600 -o heartwood -g heartwood bridge.secret /var/lib/heartwood/bridge.secret
# Docker: the image runs as uid 10001
sudo install -m 0600 -o 10001 bridge.secret /var/lib/heartwood/bridge.secret
```

### Pair a client

Pair a Nostr client with the `bunker://<master-pubkey-hex>?relay=<url>` connection string (relay URLs percent-encoded, no `secret` parameter). Get it from Sapwood, from the bridge's startup log (`sudo journalctl -u heartwood-bridge | grep 'client connection string'`), or, on the offline `provision` path, from `heartwood-bridge --bunker-uri`, which connects to the signer once, prints one string per master identity and exits without touching any relay. It reads the same configuration as the service, so give it the same `HEARTWOOD_*` values:

```bash
sudo -u heartwood env HEARTWOOD_SERIAL_PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 \
  HEARTWOOD_RELAYS=wss://relay.damus.io,wss://nos.lol heartwood-bridge --bunker-uri
```

There is no web UI or QR code served by this repo; client approval and per-client permissions are enforced on the device. See [docs/QUICKSTART.md](docs/QUICKSTART.md) for the full walkthrough.

## Key Concepts

- **TreeRoot** — the master secret derived from a 12-word BIP-39 mnemonic at path `m/44'/1237'/727'/0'/0'`. Lives only on the hardware signer.
- **Identity** — a child key derived from TreeRoot via HMAC-SHA256 keyed on `(purpose, index)`. Each purpose/index pair produces a deterministic, unique keypair.
- **Persona** — a named identity at `nostr:persona:{name}`. Convenience wrapper around `derive(root, "nostr:persona:{name}", index)`.
- **NIP-46** — the Nostr remote signing protocol used to pair clients with the hardware signer. Method dispatch, permissions, and session handling happen on the device (firmware in `heartwood-esp32`), not in this repo.
- **Linkage proof** — a BIP-340 Schnorr signature from the master key proving ownership of a child key, without revealing the derivation path (blind) or with it revealed (full).

## API Surface (Rust crates)

### heartwood-core (crate name `nsec-tree-rs`)

The directory is `crates/heartwood-core`, but the Cargo package is `nsec-tree-rs` (imported as `nsec_tree_rs`), so use `cargo test -p nsec-tree-rs`, not `-p heartwood-core`. It is published on crates.io (the release workflow runs `cargo publish -p nsec-tree-rs` on version tags; the current version is 0.1.0). Add it to `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
nsec-tree-rs = "0.1"
# or, to track this repository instead:
# nsec-tree-rs = { git = "https://github.com/forgesworn/heartwood" }
```

Signatures. Every fallible function returns `Result<_, HeartwoodError>`.

```rust
// Roots
fn from_mnemonic(mnemonic: &str, passphrase: Option<&str>) -> Result<TreeRoot, HeartwoodError>;
fn from_nsec(nsec: &str) -> Result<TreeRoot, HeartwoodError>;           // HMAC intermediate: a different root from from_mnemonic
fn from_nsec_bytes(nsec_bytes: &[u8; 32]) -> Result<TreeRoot, HeartwoodError>;
fn generate_mnemonic() -> Result<Vec<String>, HeartwoodError>;          // 24 words, OS entropy
fn npub_from_nsec(nsec: &str) -> Result<String, HeartwoodError>;        // bunker mode: no tree, no HMAC

// Derivation
fn derive(root: &TreeRoot, purpose: &str, index: u32) -> Result<Identity, HeartwoodError>;
fn derive_from_identity(identity: &Identity, purpose: &str, index: u32) -> Result<Identity, HeartwoodError>;
fn derive_persona(root: &TreeRoot, name: &str, index: Option<u32>) -> Result<Persona, HeartwoodError>;
fn derive_from_persona(persona: &Persona, purpose: &str, index: Option<u32>) -> Result<Identity, HeartwoodError>;

// Linkage proofs
fn create_blind_proof(root: &TreeRoot, child: &Identity) -> Result<LinkageProof, HeartwoodError>;
fn create_full_proof(root: &TreeRoot, child: &Identity) -> Result<LinkageProof, HeartwoodError>;
fn verify_proof(proof: &LinkageProof) -> Result<bool, HeartwoodError>;  // Ok(false) for a bad proof; Err only for unparseable hex

// Recovery
fn recover(root: &TreeRoot, purposes: &[String], scan_range: Option<u32>)
    -> Result<HashMap<String, Vec<Identity>>, HeartwoodError>;

// Encoding (bech32)
fn encode_npub(public_key: &[u8; 32]) -> String;
fn encode_nsec(private_key: &[u8; 32]) -> String;
fn decode_npub(npub: &str) -> Result<[u8; 32], HeartwoodError>;
fn decode_nsec(nsec: &str) -> Result<Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>, HeartwoodError>;
```

What the `None` arguments mean:

- `from_mnemonic(.., None)`: no BIP-39 passphrase, the same as `Some("")`. Any passphrase gives a different root. The phrase may be any valid BIP-39 length.
- `derive_persona(.., None)` and `derive_from_persona(.., None)`: index 0. `derive_persona(&root, "work", None)` equals `derive(&root, "nostr:persona:work", 0)`. `derive` and `derive_from_identity` take a plain `u32` and have no default.
- `recover(.., None)`: scan indices `0..20` for each purpose. `Some(n)` must be in `1..=10_000`, otherwise `Err(HeartwoodError::InvalidScanRange)`.
- `derive_persona` rejects an empty or whitespace-only name, `|`, and control characters with `HeartwoodError::InvalidPersonaName`.

Types:

- `TreeRoot { master_pubkey: String }`: `master_pubkey` is the bech32 `npub1...`. The secret is private; `root.destroy()` zeroises it.
- `Identity { npub: String, private_key: Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>, public_key: [u8; 32], purpose: String, index: u32 }`. `npub` is a stored field; `identity.nsec()` is a method because the bech32 nsec is computed on demand and never kept in memory.
- `Persona { identity: Identity, name: String, index: u32 }`. `index` is the resolved value, so it is `0` when `None` was passed.
- `LinkageProof { master_pubkey: String, child_pubkey: String, purpose: Option<String>, index: Option<u32>, attestation: String, signature: String }`. Unlike `TreeRoot`, the two pubkeys here are 64-character lowercase hex, not npub. `purpose` and `index` are `None` for a blind proof and `Some(..)` for a full proof. `signature` is 128 hex characters (BIP-340 Schnorr).

```rust
use nsec_tree_rs::{create_blind_proof, create_full_proof, decode_npub, decode_nsec,
                   derive, derive_from_identity, derive_from_persona, derive_persona,
                   encode_npub, encode_nsec, from_mnemonic, from_nsec, npub_from_nsec,
                   recover, verify_proof, HeartwoodError};

fn main() -> Result<(), HeartwoodError> {
    // Create a root from a BIP-39 mnemonic (placeholder words), no passphrase
    let root = from_mnemonic("word1 word2 ... word12", None)?;

    // Derive a child identity
    let identity = derive(&root, "social", 0)?;
    let nsec: String = identity.nsec(); // nsec1..., computed on demand; never log it

    // Derive a named persona, then sub-identities from an identity or a persona
    let persona = derive_persona(&root, "work", None)?;
    let sub = derive_from_identity(&identity, "notifications", 0)?;
    let dms = derive_from_persona(&persona, "dms", None)?;

    // Blind proof: proves ownership without revealing purpose or index
    let blind = create_blind_proof(&root, &identity)?;
    assert!(blind.purpose.is_none() && blind.index.is_none());
    assert!(verify_proof(&blind)?);

    // Full proof: also reveals purpose and index
    let full = create_full_proof(&root, &identity)?;
    assert_eq!(full.purpose.as_deref(), Some("social"));
    assert_eq!(full.index, Some(0));
    assert!(verify_proof(&full)?);

    // Bare nsec (bunker mode): npub only, or a root via an HMAC intermediate
    let npub = npub_from_nsec(&nsec)?;
    let nsec_root = from_nsec(&nsec)?;

    // Encoding round trips
    let public_key: [u8; 32] = decode_npub(&identity.npub)?;
    assert_eq!(encode_npub(&public_key), identity.npub);
    let private_key = decode_nsec(&nsec)?; // Zeroizing<[u8; 32]>
    assert_eq!(encode_nsec(&private_key), nsec);

    // Recover identities by scanning purposes (default: 20 indices each)
    let found = recover(&root, &["social".to_string(), "work".to_string()], None)?;
    assert_eq!(found["social"].len(), 20);
    Ok(())
}
```

This crate is a standalone reference/compatibility library now -- it is no longer a dependency of `heartwood-bridge` or of any binary in this repo. The same HMAC-SHA256 derivation scheme runs on-device, in the `heartwood-esp32` firmware.

## NIP-46 Integration (client side)

Any standard NIP-46 (Nostr Connect) client can pair with the hardware signer via the relay named in its `bunker://` or `nostrconnect://` URI -- Heartwood does not change the wire protocol clients speak. There is no Tor hidden service and no web UI; pairing, client approval, and per-client permissions are all configured on the device itself, normally via [Sapwood](https://sapwood.forgesworn.dev).

**Compatible clients:** any standard NIP-46 client. [Bark](https://github.com/forgesworn/bark) is a browser extension providing NIP-07 signing via Heartwood, built specifically for this stack.

## Security Properties

- Keys derived via HMAC-SHA256 (RFC 2104) -- not BIP-32 extended keys at the child level
- Master secret zeroed from RAM on drop (`zeroize` crate), intermediate secrets explicitly zeroised
- The bridge holds no key material and never sees plaintext -- NIP-44 decryption, NIP-46 dispatch, and signing all happen on the USB-tethered hardware signer, not the bridge
- Per-client kind restrictions, connection approval, and rate limiting are enforced on the device
- Session handling and replay protection for requests are the device's responsibility, not the bridge's
- NIP-46 messages are NIP-44 encrypted end-to-end between client and device
- `bridge.secret` authenticates the USB serial session only -- it is not a signing key; treat the file as a local secret (0600 permissions)
- No inbound listener -- the bridge only makes outbound WebSocket connections to relays; no open ports, no Tor hidden service
- NIP-42 AUTH is unsupported -- the bridge holds no key, so it cannot sign an auth challenge
- 59 tests in heartwood-core (`nsec-tree-rs`), including 5 frozen protocol vectors cross-validated against the TypeScript reference implementation

## Competitors

| Project | Platform | Multi-identity | Hardware |
|---------|----------|---------------|----------|
| **Heartwood** | Hardware signer + bridge | Yes (unlimited, unlinkable) | Yes |
| nsecBunker | VPS/server | No | No |
| Amber | Android only | No | No |
| nsec.app | Browser extension | No | No |
| LNbits NSD | Raspberry Pi | One key only | Yes |

## Ecosystem

- [nsec-tree](https://github.com/forgesworn/nsec-tree) — TypeScript reference implementation of the derivation protocol
- [shamir-words](https://github.com/forgesworn/shamir-words) — mnemonic threshold backup (Phase 2 integration)
- [canary-kit](https://github.com/forgesworn/canary-kit) — dead man's switch (pairs with Heartwood duress persona)
- [bark](https://github.com/forgesworn/bark) — browser extension for NIP-07 signing via Heartwood
- [bray](https://github.com/forgesworn/bray) — Nostr MCP server (AI agents sign through Heartwood)
